In the first five seconds after somebody says it is too expensive, most people do one of two things. They start defending the price, or they start discounting it, and both of those are answers to a question that has not been asked yet. What I do instead is ask what they are comparing it with, because too expensive is never a complete sentence. Too expensive compared with what, too expensive for whom, and too expensive over how long are three different objections, and they need three different answers. And here is the discipline that took me years. Never give a concession without asking for something in return. Not because you are being tough, but because a concession that costs the other side nothing teaches them that pushing works, and the next request arrives about forty seconds later. The negotiation gets longer, not shorter, and you end up somewhere neither side is happy with.

The last time a vendor dropped the price the moment I pushed, something happened that they probably did not expect. I stopped believing the first number, obviously, but I also did not respect the second one, because there was no reason attached to either of them. When I push back on price, most of the time I am not actually trying to pay less. I am testing whether the person in front of me understands their own number, and whether they will still be there in two years when something goes wrong. So the vendors I go back to are the ones who hold firm and tell me why. It sounds strange, but a supplier who cannot say no to me cannot say no to anybody else either, and I need somebody who can protect my project from the next customer as well.
